transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
President Trump is campaigning in Kansas today.
It comes as Republicans are pouring millions of dollars into Senate races in Kansas, Nebraska,
and Iowa.
His farmers struggle with high costs from gas prices and tariffs during harvest season.
And early voting began today in Texas.
Blaze Ganey from the Texas Newsroom reports Democrat James Tallarico is trying to draw
on Texan's love of football as he tries to flip a Republican Senate seat.
Tallarico's "Clear Eyes, Full Hearts" tour borrows from Friday Night Lights, the TV
drama about Texas high school football.
It opens Sunday in Plano, a Dallas suburb in Republican-leaning Collin County.
President Trump carried that county by more than 11 percentage points in 2024.
University of Texas researcher Josh Blank says Tallarico needs votes beyond Democratic
strongholds.
"The reality is that Democrats can win the urban and suburban parts of the state and
still lose the election if Republicans dominate the rural parts of Texas like they often do."
Tallarico faces Trump-backed Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton.
Democrats haven't won statewide in Texas in more than 30 years.
For NPR News, I'm Blaze Ganey in Austin.
The Justice Department is investigating Washington, D.C.'s jail.
The probe is examining whether conditions at the facility violate the inmates' constitutional
rights, NPR's Ryan Lucas reports.
The Justice Department's Civil Rights Division says its investigation will determine whether
the District of Columbia engages in a pattern or practice of violating the constitutional
rights of inmates at the D.C. jail.
That includes looking at whether the facility fails to protect inmates from the use of excessive
force, whether it provides inadequate medical care and nutrition, as well as unsafe and
unsanitary conditions.
There have long been allegations of poor conditions at the D.C. jail.
Just last week, inmates filed a class-action lawsuit alleging the facility provided food
with insects and mice in it.
Capitol rioters held at the jail also complained about conditions there.
Ryan Lucas, NPR News, Washington.
Iran has intensified its strikes on vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz.
Maritime monitoring shows that October has seen the highest number of shipping attacks
since the early days of the Iran War, NPR's Hadil Al-Shalchi reports.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations, or UKMTO, which is run by the British Navy, said it
logged 10 attacks in the Strait of Hormuz last week alone, including one that sank a
ship.
The monitoring group said it was "struggling" to accurately report the true number of attacks
because the majority of vessels are refusing to report them.
Iran increased its strikes on shipping vessels in the Strait of Hormuz as the U.S. tightens
its economic blockade on the country.
But oil exports have rebounded to near pre-war levels as the U.S. Navy escorts vessels through
the critical waterway.
Hadil Al-Shalchi, NPR News, Istanbul.
U.S. stocks closed mixed today.
This is NPR.
Mississippi's attorney general says a police officer in the town of Cenotobia was justified
in using force in the June shooting death of a one-year-old boy.
Cohen Wiley was killed as officers responded to a shoplifting call at a local Walmart.
The Mississippi Bureau of Investigations said their vehicle drove toward law enforcement,
at which point an officer opened fire.
Cohen's mother disputes that claim.
The Supreme Court has agreed to hear a case about a federal ban on home distilling of
liquor.
NPR's Kerry Johnson reports lower courts have split on the issue.
The case centers on a federal law from 1868 that bars people from setting up home distilleries.
Congress enacted the ban to protect tax revenue.
The Trump administration supports the post-Civil War law, arguing that billions of dollars is
at stake.
More than a dozen states led by Republicans had asked the Supreme Court to hear the issue.
People challenging the law say it amounts to overreach by Congress.
The law says home distilling is a crime that can be punished by as much as five years in
prison and a $10,000 fine.
The justices will consider the case this term with a decision expected by next summer.
Kerry Johnson, NPR News.
A former military pilot has stepped up to preserve Neil Armstrong's boyhood home in
Ohio.
Ken Schreiber donated $400,000 to the local historical society.
The organization plans to restore the home to its 1940s appearance.
The goal is to open it for public tours by 2030, marking Armstrong's 100th birthday.
This is NPR News.

topics.text: President Trump campaigns in Kansas as Republicans invest millions in Senate races in Kansas, Nebraska, and Iowa
Early voting begins in Texas as Democrat James Talarico courts voters with a football-themed tour against Ken Paxton
Justice Department opens investigation into conditions and constitutional rights at Washington, D.C.'s jail
Iran intensifies strikes on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, with October seeing the most attacks since the war began
Mississippi attorney general says Cleveland police officer was justified in fatal shooting of one-year-old Cohen Wiley
Supreme Court agrees to hear case on federal ban on home distilling of liquor
Former military pilot Ken Schreiber donates $400,000 to preserve Neil Armstrong's boyhood home in Ohio
